entries.sentence: COVID-19 is an illness caused by a virus called coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), with symptoms that overlap with colds and flu.
entries.note: NHS: illness caused by a virus called coronavirus; symptoms very similar to colds and flu. WHO names SARS-CoV-2 as the virus.

entries.sentence: COVID-19 is an infection caused by a virus that spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes.
entries.note: WHO: SARS-CoV-2 spreads through the air via infectious respiratory particles from breathing, talking, coughing, sneezing.

entries.sentence: Its symptoms are very similar to those of other illnesses such as colds and flu.
entries.note: NHS: symptoms are very similar to other illnesses such as colds and flu.

entries.sentence: Some people, including older adults and those with weakened immune systems or certain long-term conditions, are at higher risk of becoming seriously ill.
entries.note: WHO: older adults, people with underlying conditions at higher risk of severe illness; weakened immune systems listed. CDC Yellow Book: immunocompromised or underlying conditions.

entries.sentence: Some people go on to have symptoms that last for a long time, which is called long COVID.
entries.note: NHS: long COVID is when symptoms last longer than 12 weeks.

Problems with memory and concentration, often called brain fog
Heart palpitations, dizziness, and anxiety or depression during long COVID
COVID-19 can be suspected from symptoms, but these are very similar to colds and flu, so a test is used to confirm it.

entries.sentence: For people eligible for COVID-19 treatments, the NHS advises taking a rapid lateral flow test as soon as symptoms start.
Most illness is managed at home with rest and plenty of fluids, and the NHS says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be considered.
entries.note: NHS: rest, drink plenty of fluids, consider paracetamol or ibuprofen.

Antiviral medicines, including nirmatrelvir with ritonavir and molnupiravir, are offered to people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill.
Antiviral treatment has to be started early in the illness to be effective.
entries.note: CDC: treatment generally needs to start within days of symptom onset; ICB pages say the same.

entries.sentence: Vaccination helps protect against severe illness, and the UK offers a seasonal programme to the groups at highest risk.
entries.note: JCVI: older adults and immunosuppressed remain at highest risk, programme offered to them; search summary: vaccination protects against severe illness.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises staying at home and away from others when symptoms make a person feel unwell.
entries.note: NHS: stay home and away from others if high temperature or not well enough.

Contact the GP or NHS 111 if symptoms get worse or do not improve, or if a high temperature persists.
entries.note: NHS: urgent GP or NHS 111 for worsening symptoms or prolonged high temperature.

entries.sentence: People at higher risk, such as those who are pregnant, older or have a weakened immune system, are advised to get medical advice sooner.
entries.note: NHS summary lists pregnant, older, immunocompromised as higher risk to contact GP or 111 (blended).

entries.sentence: A routine GP appointment is the route for symptoms that last a long time after the infection.
entries.note: NHS: contact your GP if you think you have persistent symptoms.

entries.sentence: COVID-19 is an illness caused by a virus called coronavirus, formally SARS-CoV-2.
The virus spreads through the air in infectious respiratory particles that an infected person releases when breathing, talking, coughing or sneezing.
It can also enter the body when someone touches a contaminated surface and then touches the eyes, nose or mouth.
People are more likely to catch the virus when they are close to an infected person, or when they share a closed space with them.
An infected person can pass the virus on before any symptoms appear, and may also spread it without ever having symptoms.
entries.note: WHO: spread in absence of symptoms or in days before.

entries.sentence: WHO also describes transmission as occurring mainly from people who have symptoms, and sometimes just before they develop them.
entries.note: WHO scientific brief (WHO transmission commentary), per search summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the symptoms are very similar to those of other illnesses such as colds and flu, which can make them hard to tell apart.
The most typical ones are a high temperature, a new continuous cough, and a change in the sense of smell or taste.
The NHS also lists shortness of breath, tiredness, body aches and headache.
Some people have a sore throat, a blocked or runny nose, loss of appetite, diarrhoea or feel sick.
The NHS advises staying at home and away from other people when there is a high temperature or a person does not feel well enough to do normal activities.
Normal activities can restart once the person feels better or the temperature has gone down.
Self-care described by the NHS includes resting, drinking plenty of fluids and considering paracetamol or ibuprofen.
It also suggests avoiding lying flat on the back when coughing and not using a fan to cool the room.
WHO says older adults, people with underlying health conditions and unvaccinated people are at higher risk of severe illness.
The conditions it lists include diabetes, heart or lung disease, obesity and a weakened immune system.
Pregnant women and people with immunosuppression, such as those living with HIV, are also named as higher-risk groups.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says the risk rises with each additional underlying condition.
Health and care workers face a higher chance of exposure because of where they work.
In the UK, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation advised that older adults and people who are immunosuppressed remain at highest risk of serious disease.
For this reason, antiviral medicines through the NHS are aimed at people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill.
Rapid antigen tests give quick results and can be done at home, while PCR tests are done at testing sites or healthcare facilities.
The NHS advises people who are eligible for COVID-19 treatments to take a rapid lateral flow test as soon as symptoms start.
GOV.UK states that there are no COVID-19 restrictions in the UK and that most people cannot get free tests, though some eligible people can.
Most illness is managed at home with rest and fluids.
Antiviral medicines, such as nirmatrelvir with ritonavir (Paxlovid) and molnupiravir (Lagevrio), are offered to people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill.
Antivirals have to be started early in the illness, so a clinician decides whether a person qualifies soon after symptoms begin.
entries.note: CDC; ICB pages say start within days of symptoms. Clinician-decision wording is paraphrase.

entries.sentence: Testing can help guide treatment decisions, and a person at higher risk can ask a clinician about treatment.
entries.note: CDC: testing can guide treatment; higher-risk can ask provider.

entries.sentence: The UK runs a seasonal COVID-19 vaccination programme that offers vaccine to the groups at highest risk.
The NHS says the vaccine is available to people aged 75 and over, to some people aged 6 months to 74 with a weakened immune system, and to residents of older adult care homes.
The UKHSA states that the groups are the same across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
entries.note: Search summary of the UKHSA/GOV.UK pages.

entries.sentence: Eligibility for people with a weakened immune system depends on criteria in the Green Book, which UKHSA publishes for health professionals.
The NHS lists causes such as blood cancers, transplants, HIV and long-term immunosuppressive treatment, and says the list is only a guide, so a GP or pharmacist can advise.
entries.note: NHS page and GP practice note.

entries.sentence: Most eligible people can have the vaccine, including those who are pregnant or breastfeeding and most people with allergies.
A person with a COVID-19 infection or a high temperature is asked to wait until they feel better before vaccination.
Appointments can be booked online or in the NHS App, or through a walk-in site, without waiting for an invitation.
The JCVI noted that current vaccines give limited protection against mild infection and no evident protection against passing the virus on.
The NHS describes long COVID, also called post-COVID syndrome, as symptoms of COVID-19 that last longer than 12 weeks.
The most commonly reported symptoms are extreme tiredness, shortness of breath, joint pain and aching muscles, and problems with memory and concentration.
Having a mild first illness does not rule it out, as the chance of long-term symptoms does not seem to be linked to how ill someone was at first.
The NHS says there is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms, and physiotherapy for breathing and tiredness is one option.
entries.note: NHS; MedlinePlus: no specific treatment, care plan for symptoms.

entries.sentence: For persistent symptoms, the route is a GP appointment, and a GP may refer the person to an NHS long COVID service.
For an urgent worsening of acute illness, the NHS says to contact the GP or NHS 111 the same day.
entries.note: NHS: urgent GP or 111 for worsening symptoms.

entries.sentence: Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, or collapsing.
They are different illnesses, but the NHS says the symptoms of COVID-19 are very similar to those of colds and flu.
The most typical COVID-19 symptoms are a fever, a cough and a change in smell or taste.
Because symptoms overlap, a test is how COVID-19 is told apart, and the NHS advises a lateral flow test for people eligible for treatment.
The NHS says the vaccine is available to people aged 75 and over, to people aged 6 months to 74 with a weakened immune system, and to older adult care home residents.
The groups are the same across the UK nations.
The NHS list of conditions and treatments that weaken the immune system is a guide, and a GP or pharmacist can advise someone who is unsure.
Eligibility can change from one season to the next.
entries.note: Search summary notes eligibility has changed between seasons.

entries.sentence: Yes. WHO says an infected person can spread the virus before symptoms appear and may spread it without developing symptoms at all.
The virus passes through the air in respiratory particles from breathing, talking, coughing or sneezing.
People are more likely to catch it when close to an infected person or sharing a closed space with them.
Long COVID, also called post-COVID syndrome, is when symptoms of COVID-19 last longer than 12 weeks, according to the NHS.
Common symptoms include extreme tiredness, shortness of breath, joint pain, aching muscles and memory and concentration problems.
The NHS says there is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms.
A GP can refer someone with persistent symptoms to an NHS long COVID service.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, or collapsing.
Symptoms that are getting worse or not improving call for contact with the GP or NHS 111.
Most mild illness is managed at home with rest and fluids.
Also called: Coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2 infection
Caused by: The virus SARS-CoV-2
Typical symptoms: High temperature, new continuous cough, change in smell or taste
Spreads by: Respiratory particles in the air from breathing, talking, coughing or sneezing
Higher risk: Older adults, weakened immune system, some long-term conditions, pregnancy
Urgent help: Call 999 or A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing blood or collapse; otherwise GP or NHS 111
Vaccination: Seasonal NHS programme for the groups at highest risk
